variables.description: Mira is carrying the brass winding key of the great lamp.

variables.name: knows_code
variables.description: Mira has learned what the lamp's signals mean and how to flash a call for help.

variables.name: knows_tunnel
variables.description: Mira has studied a plan of the passages under the tower, including the keeper's own way.

variables.name: knows_ledger
variables.description: Mira has seen the tallies: cargo landed for six winters and none ever taken away.

nodes.body: Mira missed the last bus by four minutes. The fog rolled in fast, thick enough to swallow the whole headland. Somewhere ahead stood the Hollow Lighthouse. It had stood dark and empty since old keeper Ferris vanished, a year ago now, without a word. Nobody had lived there since. Nobody wanted to. But tonight, through the drifting grey, a pale light flickered in the lamp room. It blinked on, then off, like something breathing that should not be awake. Mira's feet carried her closer before her head decided anything.

choices.label: Walk down toward the light.

nodes.body: Her phone showed no bars out here, and the next bus was not until morning. "Fine," Mira told the fog, "one look, and then I sit in the shelter and behave." Four ways opened out of the mist around the old tower. The keeper's cottage crouched low against the rock, and beside it the tower stair spiraled up toward that strange glow. Under the cliff a black mouth of sea caves gaped at the tide, while the old boathouse leaned over the shingle as if it were listening.

choices.label: Try the keeper's cottage.
Climb the tower stair to the lamp room.
Slip into the sea caves under the rock.
Cross to the old boathouse.

nodes.body: Inside, the keeper's cottage was cold and still, and it smelled of salt and old paper. A mug sat on the table with a brown ring of dust where the tea had been. It looked as if Ferris had stepped out one morning a year ago and never come back. "Hello?" said Mira, and felt silly, because nobody answered and she had not wanted anybody to. A roll-top desk stood shut beneath the window. Shelves sagged along one wall under books and ships in bottles, and across the room the hearth held a heap of grey ash. Through the window the pale light went on blinking, slow as breath.

choices.label: Search the roll-top desk.
Read along the crowded shelves.
Rake through the cold hearth.

nodes.body: The roll-top rattled back with a groan, as if nobody had opened it in a year. Papers lay scattered across the desk, and on top of them sat the keeper's log, left open at its last page. The writing stopped halfway down, in the middle of a line. Under the writing surface there was one small drawer, and when Mira tugged at it, it would not move at all. Something inside slid and knocked against the wood, something small and heavy. "Locked," she said. "Of course you are."

choices.label: Read the last log page.
Work at the locked drawer.

nodes.body: The last page of the log was all in the keeper's small square hand, and every entry began with the weather. "Fog since noon," Ferris had written, "and the pale light is up again in my tower, though I did not light it and the great lamp is cold." Lower down the ink grew shaky. "He came to the door tonight, wanting the whole tower now, and me quiet. I told him" and there the line stopped, with nothing after it but a long scratch of the pen. Mira read the page twice over, and then she looked down the dark hall that led toward the tower.

choices.label: Follow the hall toward the tower.

nodes.body: The little drawer would not give, however Mira wiggled it. A bent letter-opener lay on the desk, its tip worn thin enough to slide into the keyhole, though she could tell that way would be slow. The brass handle was right there under her fingers, and the wood around it looked a hundred years old and as dry as a biscuit. Whatever was inside slid and knocked again. Out in the tower the pale light blinked, and blinked, and did not seem to be in any hurry at all.

choices.label: Pick the lock with the letter-opener.
Wrench the drawer open by its handle.

nodes.body: Mira worked the letter-opener into the lock and felt about with it, gently, the way a hand feels for a light switch in the dark. It took a dozen tries and most of her patience. Then something clicked, and the drawer slid out as if it had never been stuck. Inside lay a bundle of oilcloth, and inside that a short brass key with a square end where its teeth should be, stamped with a tiny tower. A paper tag hung from it. "Wind her slow," Mira read aloud, and wondered what on earth she was meant to wind. The key did not say, so she put it in her pocket and turned to the hall.

choices.label: Take the key down the hall.

nodes.body: The shelves sagged under ships in bottles, dozens of them, each a tiny careful world behind glass. Beside them ran a row of leather logbooks with cracked spines. Mira noticed two things almost at once. One bottled ship had a curl of paper wedged in its hull, where no sailor would put anything. And one logbook near the end of the row had a spine worn soft and shiny, as if the same hand had pulled it down night after night. "You first," she said, to both of them at once.

choices.label: Uncork the ship in the bottle.
Pull down the worn logbook.

nodes.body: The cork came out of the bottle with a soft pop, and Mira teased the paper free with one finger. It unrolled across her palm into a sketch of the tower, drawn in ink by someone with a steady hand. At the tower's foot the artist had put a small door where the wall ought to be solid stone, and beside it five words in square letters. "For whoever comes looking, please," Mira read. She looked up. The hall beyond the office ran straight toward the foot of the tower, and nobody else had come looking in a year. She folded the sketch and went.

choices.label: Take the sketch down the hall.

nodes.body: The worn logbook fell open by itself, at a page that had been read a hundred times, where a sprig of sea-holly lay pressed flat in the fold. The page was not a log at all but a list, in the keeper's square hand, underlined so hard that the pen had torn the paper. "The pale light is his, not mine," it said. "Steady, he lands; blinking, he keeps off; and three short, three long, three short will bring any keeper on this coast." Mira looked out of the window at the tower, where the light was blinking. "Keeps off who?" she said, and she took the question with her down the hall.

choices.label: Follow the hall toward the blinking light.

nodes.body: The hearth was cold and heaped with pale ash. Mira crouched and pushed her fingers through it, and near the back, where the fire had never burned hot enough, they met something stiff and square. Above it one firebrick sat crooked in the wall, a finger's width out of line with its neighbours, as if it had been pulled loose and pushed back in a hurry. Soot sifted down when she touched it. "One of you is hiding something," she told the fireplace. "Possibly both."

choices.label: Sift the ash for the square thing.
Work the loose firebrick free.

nodes.body: The square thing in the ash was a photograph, scorched brown along one edge but whole enough to read. An old man in a keeper's cap stood on the lamp gallery beside a younger one in a good coat, and only the keeper was smiling. Someone had tried to burn it and had not stayed to watch it catch. Mira turned it over. On the back, in small square letters, it said: "V. and self, the first winter. I should have shut the door." She slid the photograph into her pocket and stood up, and the dark hall to the tower seemed longer than it had a minute ago.

choices.label: Carry the photograph to the hall.

nodes.body: Mira got her fingertips around the loose firebrick and pulled, and it slid halfway out with a gritty scrape. Behind it was a hollow, and in the hollow, just in reach, sat a small bundle wrapped in oilcloth. Then the brick jammed, half in and half out, and when she reached past it the rough edge bit her knuckles. Above her the bricks of the chimney shifted very slightly, with a sound like someone clearing their throat. "Don't," Mira told the chimney.

choices.label: Ease the bundle out past the brick.
Yank the jammed brick out of the way.

nodes.body: Mira flattened her hand and slid it past the brick a little at a time, and the bundle came out with nothing worse than a scraped thumb. She unwound the oilcloth. Inside lay a short brass key, cool and heavy, with a square end where its teeth should be and a tiny tower stamped on its bow. A paper tag was tied to it. "Wind her slow," she read. It was not the key to any door she had ever seen. Whoever hid it had wanted it found, though, by somebody careful, and Mira closed her fingers round it and went down the hall.

choices.label: Follow the hall with the key.

nodes.body: The hall was narrow and unlit, and the floorboards told on her at every step. At its far end stood the tower's inner door, a heavy shape with a line of pale light flickering underneath it, on and off. Halfway along, a side passage opened toward the kitchen, and a thin cold draught came out of it and stirred the dust along the floor. It smelled of wet stone and the sea. That was an odd thing for a kitchen to smell of. Mira stopped between them, with the light blinking ahead of her and the draught breathing on her ankles.

choices.label: Go straight to the tower door.
Follow the draught into the kitchen.

nodes.body: The draught came from the pantry. Mira followed it past shelves of rusted tins to the back wall of the kitchen, where the cold breathed up through a crack between the flagstones. Above the crack, somebody had drawn on the plaster in pencil, patiently, over what must have been many evenings. It was a plan of everything under the tower: a brick tunnel, a room, a store, a sea gate, and one thin line marked "my way" that ran from behind a lantern bracket up to the moor. "So that is where the wind comes from," Mira said. She studied the plan until she could have drawn it herself.

choices.label: Go back to the tower door.

nodes.body: The tower door stood ajar, and cold air leaned on it from the other side. Mira pushed it open onto a low stone landing at the foot of the tower. There was nothing here but a three-legged stool, and on the stool a battered journal, lying open as if somebody had only just put it down. Dust lay thick on the floor all around. It did not lie on the journal. "That," said Mira quietly, "is not a year old." She crossed the landing and reached for it.

choices.label: Pick up the journal.

nodes.body: The tower stair wound up and up until Mira's legs burned, and at the top she stepped into the lamp room. The pale light was here, pulsing on and off, but it gave no heat and she could see no flame. It seemed to come out of the floor. The great glass lens stood in the middle of the room like a huge unlit jewel, and a narrow door led out to the gallery walk, where the fog pressed against the glass. To one side hung a clockwork weight on a long chain, the engine that had once turned the lamp all night. "Somebody is doing this," Mira said, "because lights do not just happen."

choices.label: Examine the great glass lens.
Step toward the gallery walk.
Study the clockwork weight.

nodes.body: Up close, the great lens was not lit at all. The glow came from below, thrown up through a cracked panel near its base, and it turned Mira's hands the colour of seawater. She leaned around the brass housing and found something stranger. A second mirror, small and new, had been bolted in behind the old one, where nothing was ever meant to sit. Something hung on a nail behind that mirror too, wrapped in a twist of oilcloth and well out of sight. The crack breathed cold air up at her, and far down inside it something ticked.

choices.label: Look down through the cracked panel.
Reach behind the hidden mirror.

nodes.body: Mira put her eye to the cracked panel and looked down. Below her a shaft ran straight through the heart of the tower, like a stone throat, and the pale light climbed up it from somewhere deep, blinking on and blinking off. Then, while it was on, something crossed in front of it, slowly, and for a second the whole shaft went dark in the shape of a shoulder. Mira jerked back so fast that she sat down. "Not a ghost," she whispered, "because ghosts do not have shoulders." A narrow stair curled down beside the lens, and after a long moment she made herself take it.

choices.label: Take the stair down.

nodes.body: The hidden mirror was tilted to catch a light from far below and throw it up into the lamp room, where the big lens would spread it out to sea. It was a trick, and a clever one. Mira reached behind it and unhooked the bundle from its nail. Inside the oilcloth lay a short brass key with a square end instead of teeth, stamped with a tiny tower, and a tag that said "Wind her slow." It fitted nothing on the mirror. "Then what are you for?" she asked it, and put it in her pocket. A narrow stair curled down beside the lens, toward wherever the light began.

choices.label: Take the key down the stair.

nodes.body: The gallery walk ran round the outside of the lamp room, open to the night. Wind tugged at Mira's jacket the moment she cracked the door. The iron rail along the edge was furred with rust, and a flake of it came away on her thumb like a dead leaf. Below, the fog was so thick that she could not see the rocks, only hear the sea working at them a long way down. Out past the rail, low on the water, she thought something had winked. The window beside the door was fogged nearly white.

choices.label: Step out onto the walk.
Wipe the fogged window and look.

nodes.body: Mira stepped out onto the walk, one foot and then the other. The iron grating hummed in the wind, and when her hand brushed the rail it shivered along its whole length. The tower wall behind her was cold and solid. Out on the water the wink came again, a small yellow spark, low down, exactly where no light had any business being. The far side of the walk faced straight out to sea. The rail was an arm's length away, and the spark was just beyond the place where the fog began.

choices.label: Keep her back to the wall and edge round.
Lean out on the rail for a better look.

nodes.body: She kept her back to the wall and went round with her shoulder blades scraping the stone, and she did not touch the rail once. On the seaward side the fog thinned for the space of three breaths. A boat lay out there, long and grey and showing one small yellow lamp, holding still against the tide as if it were tied to the tower by a string. Each time the pale light above her blinked, a figure in the bow lifted something to its face. "You are watching it too," Mira said. Then the fog shut, and she felt her way back to the door and the stair down.

choices.label: Go back in and take the stair down.

nodes.body: Mira rubbed a clear patch in the fogged window with her sleeve and put her nose to it. There was nothing to see out at sea but grey. Straight down, though, low on the tower's side, a thin green glow leaked out of a small window, and it blinked in time with the light above her head. So the light was not up here at all. It began somewhere low in the tower and only climbed up to show itself, the way smoke climbs a chimney. "Down, then," Mira said, and turned to look for the stair.

choices.label: Head for the stair down.

nodes.body: The clockwork weight hung on a chain as thick as Mira's wrist, and both were stiff with rust. This was the engine that had once turned the great lamp through every night of the year. She gave the chain a tug, and deep in the works something groaned as if it remembered how to move. In the side of the gear case there was a square brass socket, the size of a coin, where a key ought to go, and it was empty. The chain itself ran down through a slot in the floor, into a shaft with a narrow keepers' stair beside it.

choices.label: Haul on the chain to wind it.
Follow the chain down the keepers' stair.

nodes.body: Mira wrapped both hands round the chain and hauled until the mechanism groaned, held, and turned one grinding notch that shook dust out of the ceiling. Nothing lit, because the great lamp wanted its key, and all her hauling had done was wake the noise. It rang down through the tower like a dropped bucket, and when it faded she heard something else, far below: quick footsteps, and a door closing. "Hello?" Mira called, before she could stop herself, but nobody answered. The pale light went on blinking, and the stair beside the chain led down toward the place where the footsteps had been.

choices.label: Go down the stair beside the chain.

nodes.body: The keepers' stair wound down beside the chain shaft, and its wall was covered in painted signs, the old official ones, flaking now: fog signal, ship aground, pilot wanted. Below them someone had added three lines in fresh pencil, and Mira held her phone up to read them. "Pale light, his," she read. "Steady, he lands; blinking, he keeps off; and three short, three long, three short will bring any keeper on this coast." She looked up the shaft at the blinking glow. "Keep off," she said slowly, "so it is telling somebody to keep off."

choices.label: Carry on down the keepers' stair.

nodes.body: The stair came out on a cramped iron landing, a third of the way down the tower, and here the way split. A spiral stair went on round the inside of the wall, each step worn into a shallow dish by a hundred years of keepers' boots. Beside it a service hatch stood open in the floor, with iron rungs dropping straight down a shaft no wider than a chimney. Warm air rose out of the hatch, and with it came a smell that made Mira stop and sniff twice. It was pipe smoke, and it was fresh.

choices.label: Wind down the spiral stair.
Climb down through the service hatch.

nodes.body: The spiral stair went down for what felt like forever, and Mira counted steps to keep her mind off the dark. At ninety-one it let her out on a low stone landing at the very foot of the tower. There was nothing here but a three-legged stool, and on the stool a battered journal, lying open as if somebody had only just put it down. Dust lay thick on the floor all around it. None lay on the journal. "That is not a year old," Mira said quietly, and she crossed the landing to the stool.

choices.label: Pick up the journal.

nodes.body: The rungs under the service hatch took Mira down through the tower's hollow core, past pipes and the long still chain. Halfway down they passed a brass plate bolted to the stone. It was the builders' plan of the foundations. Somebody had gone over it since in pencil, adding a brick tunnel, a room, a store, a sea gate, and one thin line marked "my way" that ran up to the moor. Mira hung there and learned it by heart. Then the shaft let her out, breathing hard, on a low landing at the tower's foot. A battered journal lay open on a stool there, with no dust on it at all.

choices.label: Take up the journal.

nodes.body: Under the rock, the sea caves breathed with the tide. Cold air sighed in and out with every wave, and the dark was full of dripping and the slow hiss of water on stone. Mira stood on the edge of a shallow pool with her phone held up for a torch. A wet passage ran inland, under the headland, with the sea already licking along its floor. To one side a rock shelf held a scatter of tide pools that glimmered faintly green by themselves. Straight ahead stood a low arch, and somebody had scratched it all over with marks.

choices.label: Follow the wet passage inland.
Search the glimmering tide pools.
Read the marks on the arch.

nodes.body: The passage narrowed fast, until Mira could touch both walls. Water slid over the toes of her boots and then drew back, and each time it came a little higher than before. The tide was on its way in. Along the left-hand wall ran a ledge, slimy but dry on top and just wide enough for careful feet, and it climbed as it went. Down the middle the floor ran flat and easy and ankle deep, straight toward a faint green glow at the far end. "It is only water," Mira said, and did not sound sure.

choices.label: Climb onto the ledge and follow it in.
Wade straight down the middle.

nodes.body: Mira climbed onto the ledge and went along it sideways, like a crab, with her back flat to the wet rock. Below her the water came up the passage in long quiet pushes, and soon the floor she might have walked on was gone under a metre of black sea. "Good choice, Mira," she said. "Well done, Mira." The ledge climbed above the tideline and widened into a shelf of dry stone. From there a flight of steps had been cut into the rock, and on the bottom step, in the wet, was the print of a large boot that had not been there long enough to dry.

choices.label: Take the cut steps up.

nodes.body: The tide pools lay along the shelf like a row of dropped coins. Each was fringed with a weed that glowed, faintly, the exact pale green of the light on the tower. It was cold to look at and rather beautiful. In the largest pool something else showed under the water, a dull gleam of brass half buried in sand and broken shell. An empty glass jar stood on the rock beside the pool, with a rag of the same weed dried to its rim. Somebody had been collecting here, and not long ago.

choices.label: Scoop up the glowing weed.
Fish out the gleam of brass.

nodes.body: The glowing weed sat in Mira's cupped hands like cold green fire that did not burn and did not go out. She held it up beside her phone and watched the white torchlight turn the same drowned colour as the light on the tower. "That is how you do it," she said, "with a lamp, and a jar of this in front of it." Nobody haunted anything, then, and somebody came down here with a jam jar. She let the weed slide back into its pool, wiped her hands on her jeans, and found a rope handrail leading up the rock toward a stair.

choices.label: Follow the handrail up.

nodes.body: Mira pushed her sleeve up and reached into the cold for the gleam of brass. What came out was a short key on a broken chain, with a keeper's tide badge still linked to it. The key had a square end where its teeth should be, and a tiny tower stamped on its bow. It looked as if it had been dropped in a hurry, by someone running, and she wondered which way they had been running. "Finders keepers," Mira said, and then thought about who the keeper was and felt strange. She put it in her pocket. Beyond the pools a stair climbed out of the cave.

choices.label: Climb the rock stair with the key.

nodes.body: The arch was scratched all over with tally marks, in fives, row upon row. Under them ran three lines of cramped writing that Mira would have to work at. Whoever made them had stood here many times, with a nail or a knife, counting something. Beyond the arch the cave pinched in to a narrow gap between two slabs of rock, barely wider than her shoulders, and cold air whistled through it from somewhere higher up. The sea slapped at the entrance pool behind her. It was louder than it had been.

choices.label: Count the tally marks and read the writing.
Squeeze into the narrow gap.

nodes.body: Mira counted the tally marks with her finger, lost her place twice, and made it forty-three. Under them the cramped writing said: "Every fog night. Steady, he lands; blinking, he keeps off; and three short, three long, three short will bring any keeper." The last tally was so fresh that grey rock dust still clung in the scratch. "Forty-three nights of what?" Mira asked the arch, and she looked back through the cave mouth at the pale light, blinking away up there in the fog. Past the arch, an arrow scratched in the rock pointed to a stair going up.

choices.label: Follow the arrow to the stair.

nodes.body: The gap was tight and bitterly cold. Mira turned sideways and got one arm and one of her shoulders into it before the rock closed on her chest and her back together. She could feel her heartbeat against the stone. Ahead the gap ran on, no wider, toward a grey smudge that might have been open air. A draught came through it, and with the draught came a sound, slow and regular, like a very large clock. Behind her, to the left of the slabs, her groping hand had brushed the edge of another opening.

choices.label: Back out and try the other opening.
Breathe out and force her shoulders through.

nodes.body: Mira let all her breath go and began to back out of the gap a finger's width at a time, which took far longer than getting in had. Then she felt along the rock to the left of the slabs until her hand found the other opening again. It was a low crawl, dry underfoot, that climbed steeply away from the sea with the draught coming down it. She went up it on her hands and knees until the roof lifted and she could stand.

choices.label: Climb on up the crawl.

nodes.body: The way climbed out of the reach of the sea, and the air turned dry and still. Mira came up into a round chamber directly under the tower, where the roar of the tide was only a mutter in the floor. A flight of steps wound up one side of it, worn smooth in the middle. Beside them an iron ladder was bolted straight up the rock, into a shaft where a small brass plate caught the light of her phone. A burnt match lay on the bottom step. Mira picked it up, and it still smelled of smoke. "Who strikes a match in a cave," she asked the dark, "and when?"

choices.label: Take the worn steps.
Climb the iron ladder past the plate.

nodes.body: The worn steps wound up through the rock, and every one of them had a wet bootprint on it, pointing the same way she was going. Mira put her own foot beside one and found the print nearly twice the size. "Big feet and dry socks," she whispered, "so lucky you." The steps let her out on a low stone landing inside the foot of the tower. There was nothing on it but a three-legged stool, and on the stool a battered journal, lying open, with no dust on it at all. The bootprints went up to the stool and stopped.

choices.label: Pick up the journal.

nodes.body: The iron ladder took Mira up a shaft like a chimney, and halfway up she came level with the brass plate. It was the builders' plan of the tower's foundations. Somebody had gone over it since in pencil, adding a brick tunnel, a room, a store, a sea gate, and one thin line marked "my way" that ran up to the moor. Mira hooked an arm through the ladder and learned it by heart. Then she climbed on, arms aching, and pulled herself out onto a low landing at the tower's foot. A battered journal lay open on a stool there, with no dust on it at all.

choices.label: Take up the journal.

nodes.body: The old boathouse leaned so far over that Mira half expected it to fall down when she opened the door. It smelled of tar and rope and salt, and the wind came through the gaps in the planks and made the whole place creak like a ship. A dinghy lay beached in one corner under a stiff canvas tarp. A tool locker stood against the wall on hinges rusted orange. Overhead, a ladder with several rungs missing climbed to a dark loft under the roof. "Right," said Mira, rubbing her cold hands. "Where would I hide something?"

choices.label: Search the beached dinghy.
Open the tool locker.
Climb the ladder to the loft.

nodes.body: Mira lifted a corner of the tarp and looked into the dinghy. A set of oilskins lay folded on the thwart, and they were dry and smelled of pipe smoke, which was strange for a boat nobody had used in a year. Further in, under the stiff canvas, the edge of a rolled chart showed pale in the gloom. Up in the bow sat a bailing tin with its lid jammed on, and when she nudged it with her foot, something inside slid and clinked. It did not sound like water.

choices.label: Pull the tarp back and unroll the chart.
Prise the lid off the bailing tin.

nodes.body: The tarp crackled back like a sail. Mira unrolled the chart across the thwart and pinned its corners with her elbows. It showed this headland, and somebody had inked in everything that lay under it: a passage from the boathouse to the tower, a brick tunnel, a room, a store, a sea gate, and one thin line marked "my way" running up to the moor. She traced each of them twice with her finger. "You could walk right under the lighthouse," she said, "and nobody would ever know." In the corner of the boathouse, half under a heap of old net, was the floor hatch the chart began at.

choices.label: Cross to the floor hatch.

nodes.body: The lid of the bailing tin came off with a squeal. Inside lay a short brass key with a square end where its teeth should be, stamped with a tiny tower, and under it a scrap of paper in small square handwriting. "The light is not a ghost, it is a signal," Mira read aloud, "and if you have come this far, come further, and wind her slow." She turned the paper over, but that was all, and the boathouse had nothing to add about who was to be wound. The key went into her pocket with the note. In the corner, half under a heap of old net, she could see the edge of a hatch in the floor.

choices.label: Go to the floor hatch.

nodes.body: The locker's hinges shrieked as Mira dragged it open. Inside hung a coil of good rope, still pale and strong. Beside it stood a storm lantern that sloshed when she lifted it, half full of oil, with a box of dry matches tucked behind the handle. The back wall of the locker was covered in chalk, rows and rows of it, too faint to read in this light. The boathouse was very dark, and the far end of it, where the floor sounded hollow, was darker still.

choices.label: Take the coil of rope.
Light the storm lantern.

nodes.body: Mira knotted one end of the rope to the ring by the door and paid the rest out behind her as she crossed the boathouse, the way cave divers do. If the dark got too thick she could always follow it back. "Clever," she told herself, "nervous, but clever." The floor boomed under her boots near the far wall. She knelt and swept aside a heap of old net, and found a wooden hatch with an iron ring, its edges worn pale by years of hands. She tied off the rope beside it, so that the way out was marked.

choices.label: Take hold of the hatch ring.

nodes.body: The third match caught, and the lantern's warm light rolled across the locker's back wall. The chalk was a tally. "Landed, fog," it said at the top, in small square writing, and under that ran six winters of marks, each with a number of crates beside it and the letter V. A second column was headed "Taken away." It was empty from top to bottom. "So it all came in," Mira said slowly, "and none of it ever went out." She hung the lantern on a nail by the locker, where its light reached the far corner. Under a heap of old net there, it found the edge of a hatch in the floor.

choices.label: Cross to the hatch in the lantern light.

nodes.body: The ladder to the loft had more gaps than rungs. Mira shook it, and it rattled against the beam but stayed where it was. Near the top, exactly where she would need to put her weight to swing herself up, one rung was cracked right across and held together by paint. Above it the loft was a square of deeper dark. Something pale was pinned to a beam up there, a big sheet of paper covered in dots and lines, and it flapped once in the draught as if it were waving.

choices.label: Climb slowly and step over the cracked rung.
Go up fast and trust the cracked rung.

nodes.body: Mira climbed slowly, like a spider, testing each rung twice, and stepped clean over the cracked one. The loft was stuffed with signal flags, faded to the colours of old sweets. The sheet pinned to the beam was a chart of lamp signals, long flashes and short ones, and across the bottom someone had added three lines in pencil. "Pale light, his," Mira read. "Steady, he lands; blinking, he keeps off; and three short, three long, three short will bring any keeper." She said it over until it stuck. A trapdoor at the back let her down beside a hatch in the boathouse floor.

choices.label: Drop down beside the floor hatch.

nodes.body: The hatch had an iron ring, and it did not want to come up. Mira got both hands through the ring and heaved, and it lifted a finger's width and stuck, breathing cold air at her out of the dark underneath. "Not now," she said through her teeth, because behind her the boathouse door had started to bang. The wind had got its fingers round it, and each slam shook the whole leaning shed and brought dust and bits of old birds' nest down from the rafters. A shelf of heavy gear above the hatch jumped on its brackets every time.

choices.label: Keep heaving until the hatch comes up.
Go back and wedge the banging door.

nodes.body: Mira kept heaving, and the hatch came up all at once and nearly sat her down. Stone steps led under the floor into a passage that ran, low and straight, beneath the rock toward the tower. She went along it bent double, with her phone held out in front of her like a candle. Halfway, she smelled pipe smoke. At the end the passage opened onto a low landing at the tower's foot, and she straightened up with a groan. There was nothing here but a three-legged stool, and a battered journal lying open on it, without a speck of dust.

choices.label: Take up the journal.

nodes.body: The journal was the keeper's own, with "Ferris, his book" written inside the cover in small square handwriting. Mira sat down on the stool with it and turned the pages by the light of her phone. Three things were tangled together in it. Some pages worried at a pale light that burned on fog nights when no lamp was lit, and some were ruled into a ledger of cargoes landed after dark. Near the back, a hurried sketch showed a tunnel under the tower. Somewhere over her head, inside the wall, a floorboard creaked and then was very quiet.

choices.label: Read the entries about the pale light.
Study the ledger of night cargoes.
Turn to the sketch of the tunnel.

nodes.body: The entries about the pale light grew more uneasy the further Mira read, and every one of them began with the weather. "Fog. The pale light is up and I did not light it," Ferris had written, and a week later, "Fog. It is up again. I have stopped telling myself it is the moon." Two pages were different from the rest. On one he had set out, carefully, exactly how the light behaved and what he thought each kind of shining meant. On the other he had ruled a column of dates, dozens of them, with a short note beside each. The newest ink in that column looked very black.

choices.label: Read what the light's shining means.
Run a finger down the column of dates.

nodes.body: "I have watched the light thirty nights now," the page began, "and it is no ghost but a lantern and mirrors, hidden in my own tower, and its shining means something to a boat." Below that, Ferris had made a list. "Steady, he lands; blinking, he keeps off; and that is all his code. Mine is older: three short, three long, three short, and any keeper on this coast will come." Mira looked up toward the light she had followed here through the fog, on and off, on and off. Here it was in the keeper's own hand, and it meant what it had meant all night: somebody out there was being told to keep off. The last line was underlined twice, and it said: "Take the stair behind the panel."

choices.label: Look for the panel and the stair.

nodes.body: Mira ran her finger down the column, and every date in it was a fog night. Beside each, for six winters, Ferris had noted crates landed, signed for with the letter V, and the space he had ruled for crates taken away again stayed empty all the way down. Then came a gap, where the keeper had vanished. After the gap the dates went on, for a whole year more, in the same square hand, with only one word beside each: "Blinking." Mira's finger stopped on the last one. It was today's date, and the ink smeared when she touched it. "You were here," she whispered. "You were here tonight." A note in the margin said: "Stair behind the panel."

choices.label: Find the panel and the stair.

nodes.body: There was only one wall on the landing that a panel could hide in. Mira went along it rapping with her knuckles, feeling foolish, until the stone answered with a sound like a wooden box. She pressed. A section of the wall swung inward on hinges that somebody kept oiled, without the smallest squeak, and behind it a cramped stair went up into the thickness of the tower. Cold air came down it, and a regular ticking, and the faint green flicker of the light. "Take the stair," Mira reminded herself. "He did say."

choices.label: Climb the stair behind the panel.

nodes.body: The ledger pages were ruled as neatly as a shop's accounts. Down the left ran fog nights, six winters of them. Beside each was a count of the cargo landed, in crates and barrels, and beside that, where a signature should be, one letter: V. A last column was headed "Taken away," and it was blank from the top of the first page to the bottom of the last. "All in," Mira said, "and nothing out. Where did you put it all?" Small figures crowded the margins, added up and crossed through. Here and there the single V had been written out longer, as a name, in a kind of code.

choices.label: Add up the cargo figures.
Puzzle out the coded name.

nodes.body: Mira added up the figures on her phone, twice, and got the same answer both times. Four hundred and twelve crates had come in under this tower. Not one was marked as leaving. Stranger still, a page had been torn out near the back, so roughly that a strip of it was left in the binding with half a drawing on it: a corner of brickwork, an arrow, the word "store." The totals sat there on the page in the keeper's square hand, the kind of numbers a harbour master would very much like to see.

choices.label: Copy the totals into her phone.
Hunt for the torn-out page.

nodes.body: Mira photographed every page of the ledger and then, because phones die, copied the totals onto the back of her hand in biro as well. Six winters. Four hundred and twelve crates. One letter. "Somebody ran a shop in a lighthouse," she said, "and never sold anything." It made no sense yet, but it was proof, and proof was worth having. At the foot of the last page the keeper had written a line that had nothing to do with crates. "If you have read this far," it said, "there is a stair behind the panel."

choices.label: Look for the panel and the stair.

nodes.body: The torn-out page had not gone far. It was folded small and pushed down inside the journal's back cover, and Mira worked it out with a fingernail. On one side Ferris had written, "His store is under my feet and I have never once looked in it." On the other he had drawn what lay beneath the tower: a brick tunnel, a room, a store, a sea gate, and one thin line marked "my way" that climbed to the moor. She studied it until she could shut her eyes and still see it. At the bottom he had added: "The stair behind the panel goes to all of it."

choices.label: Look for the panel and the stair.

nodes.body: The coded name was written in a child's code, every letter swapped for the one after it, and Mira had it broken in the time it takes to eat an apple. V was a man named Varley. "Paid by Varley," said the small notes down the margin, and "Varley, for looking the other way," winter after winter, with a sum of money beside each. The last note was different. "He does not want my blind eye now. He wants my tower. I have said no and I am afraid." Mira's stomach tightened. Under it, in darker ink, the keeper had written: "Stair behind the panel."

choices.label: Look for the panel and the stair.

nodes.body: The panel was easy to find once she knew to look. One stretch of the landing wall sounded hollow under her knuckles, and when Mira pressed it, it swung inward on oiled hinges and showed her a cramped stair going up. But there was a second door on the landing too, low and iron-bound, tucked in the corner where the shadows were thickest. It had a padlock on it as big as her fist. Everything else in this tower was rusty. The padlock was new, and bright, and somebody had oiled it.

choices.label: Take the stair behind the panel.
Rattle the new padlock on the low door.

nodes.body: The sketch near the back was drawn fast, with a pen that had spluttered. It showed the tower from the side, cut open like a cake, with a tunnel running out beneath it toward the sea. There was a great deal of small writing on it that would take time to read. At the foot of the drawing Ferris had inked a little cross, and written "under the stone" beside it. Mira looked down. One of the landing's flagstones, an arm's length from the stool, had the same small cross cut into its corner, and it rocked when she put her foot on it.

choices.label: Study the tunnel sketch properly.
Lift the corner of the marked flagstone.

nodes.body: Mira bent over the sketch with her phone until the small writing came clear. Under the tower ran a brick tunnel that split three ways, to a room marked "mine," a store marked "his," and a sea gate. Wavy lines showed where the tide got in. One more line, thin as a hair, was marked "my way," and it ran from behind a lantern bracket up to the moor. The only way down to any of it began with a stair, drawn inside the tower wall, behind a panel on this very landing. She learned the whole plan by heart before she looked up.

choices.label: Find the panel on the landing.

nodes.body: The corner of the marked flagstone came up a hand's width, and Mira's fingers found a slate lying in the hollow underneath. She drew it out and found that the keeper had scratched a list on it. "Steady, he lands; blinking, he keeps off," it said, "and three short, three long, three short will bring any keeper." She read it through twice, slowly, under her breath. Below the slate the hollow went on down, dark and wet-smelling, and the big stone ground against its neighbours when she leaned on it. The sketch lay open on the stool behind her.

choices.label: Leave the stone and study the sketch.
Heave the flagstone right over.

nodes.body: Mira got both hands under the edge and heaved, and the flagstone went over with a boom that she felt in her teeth. Under it was a square shaft, lined with green slime, with black water moving at the bottom. A rusted ladder went down into the water and did not come up again. "No, thank you," said Mira, "but no." The noise was still rolling round the tower. When it died she heard, above her and inside the wall, three quick footsteps and then nothing. She backed away from the hole until her shoulders met the landing wall, and the wall moved.

choices.label: Turn round to the wall that moved.

nodes.body: A panel in the landing wall swung inward at a touch, on hinges that somebody kept oiled, and did not make a sound. Behind it a cramped stair went up into the thickness of the tower. Cold air came down it, and a slow steady ticking, and the green flicker of the light going on and off. Mira ducked under the low frame. The stone pressed close on both sides and smelled of salt and, very faintly, of pipe smoke. "After you," she said to nobody, and wished at once that she had not.

choices.label: Climb to where the stair divides.

nodes.body: A dozen steps up, the stair came to a tiny landing and divided. To the left it went on inside the wall, a tight winding stair that climbed into the dark like the inside of a shell. To the right it went out through a slit of a door onto steps that ran up the outside of the tower, with the fog on one side and the sea somewhere under it. The ticking was louder here. It came down from above, slow and patient, and between the ticks Mira heard a small sound like a shutter falling. Each time it fell, the light went out.

choices.label: Take the tight winding stair.
Climb the outer steps in the fog.

nodes.body: The winding stair was so narrow that Mira's shoulders brushed both walls. She kept one hand on the cold stone and counted steps, because counting was better than thinking about who else might be on them. Most rang solid. The nineteenth did not. It gave a hollow knock under her boot, like a lid, and when she shifted her weight something inside it slid and rustled. She stopped with a foot on either side of that step. Above her the ticking went on, and the shutter fell, and the light went out and came back.

choices.label: Step over it and climb on.
Stamp on the step to see what is inside.

nodes.body: Mira stretched a long leg over the hollow step and climbed on, and left it to its secret. From there she kept to the wall side of every tread and tested each before she trusted it, and the stair held. It ended at a small door of frosted glass. Green light pulsed behind it, on and off, and through the glass came the slow tick she had been following all the way up. The door was warm under her palm. "Lamps are warm," Mira told herself, "and that is all it is." She stood a moment with her heart going hard, and then she reached for the handle.

choices.label: Open the frosted door.

nodes.body: The outer steps hugged the side of the tower, slick with damp and open on the left to nothing at all. Mira kept her right hand flat on the stone and went up sideways. Halfway, a gust came round the tower like a shove from a big hand, and she had to press her whole body to the wall until it let go of her. Fog streamed past her face. Somewhere below and inland, she thought, a door banged. The steps went on up into the grey, and the wind was already gathering itself for another try.

choices.label: Push on up the steps between the gusts.
Wait against the wall for the wind to drop.

nodes.body: Mira flattened herself against the wall and waited, counting her breaths. At forty the wind dropped, quite suddenly, and the fog thinned with it. For a moment she could see the whole dark slope of the headland behind the lighthouse. A small yellow light was moving up it, away from the tower, toward the moor. It swung as it went, the way a lantern swings in the hand of somebody walking, and it was not hurrying. Mira shouted after it, but the fog closed over it like a lid. She looked up at the steps still to climb, with her mind going a great deal faster than her feet.

choices.label: Climb on to the top of the steps.

nodes.body: The steps ended on a ledge no bigger than a doormat, in front of a small door of frosted glass. Mira arrived at it out of breath, with her fingers stiff and her hair stuck to her face. Green light pulsed behind the glass, on and off, and she could hear the slow tick of whatever was making it. The door was warm when she laid her hand on it. "Lamps are warm," she told herself, "and that is all it is." The wind tried one last shove at her back, and she reached for the handle.

choices.label: Open the frosted door.

nodes.body: Mira opened the frosted door, and the ghost of the Hollow Lighthouse turned into a lantern on a shelf. It was an ordinary storm lantern, burning behind a jar of something green that glowed. A ring of angled mirrors caught its light and threw it up a shaft toward the lamp room. In front of it a tin shutter rose and fell, worked by a little clockwork motor, tick, tick, clack. On, off. "You are a machine," Mira told it. "I walked all this way for a machine." But clockwork runs down, and somebody had wound this tonight and filled the lantern too. Three ways led down from the chamber: a broad stone stair, a narrow service shaft, and a ladder outside in the fog.

choices.label: Go down the stone stair.
Climb down the service shaft.
Take the outer ladder down.

nodes.body: The stone stair was broad and dry, and after everything else tonight it felt like a pavement. Partway down it widened into a landing with a cupboard built into the wall, its door hanging open a hand's width. Inside, Mira could see coils of wire, a wooden box, and the sleeve of a heavy coat. A saucer on the cupboard shelf held a little heap of pipe ash, and when she put a finger to it she snatched the finger back. "That is warm," she said, though nothing had any business being warm in a tower where nobody lived. Below her the stair went on down, and nothing moved on it.

choices.label: Go on down the stair.
Open the cupboard wide.

nodes.body: Mira went on down the stair, quicker now and much quieter, with the back of her neck prickling. It wound past the wires and mirrors of the rig and on into colder air. At the bottom it opened into a low undercroft with walls that sweated. Ahead, a round brick tunnel mouth breathed at her, in and out, like something asleep. She stood at the edge of it and listened for footsteps. There was only the sea, a long way off, and the tick of the clockwork far above.

choices.label: Step into the tunnel mouth.

nodes.body: The cupboard held more than she expected. The wooden box contained a spare lens wrapped in flannel, its glass scored with fine lines like the ones on the mirrors upstairs. The coat was a keeper's storm coat, heavy as a wet dog, and it smelled of pipe smoke, not old smoke but tonight's. One pocket hung lower than the other, as if there were something in it. "He was standing right here," Mira said, and looked over her shoulder at the empty stair. She wanted to be quick about it, and gone.

choices.label: Unwrap the spare lens.
Search the pocket of the keeper's coat.

nodes.body: The spare lens was the size of a saucer and far heavier than it looked. The lines cut into it matched the mirrors on the rig exactly, and when Mira held it up to her phone the light came through in a tight green bar. So it was a spare part, which meant that somebody mended this thing. Somebody kept it going, with spares and oil and a cupboard to keep them in, the way people keep a bicycle going. "The ghost has a job," Mira said. She wrapped the lens up again, put it back, and went on down to where the stair met the tunnel.

choices.label: Go on down to the tunnel.

nodes.body: The pocket of the coat held a box of matches, a twist of tobacco, and a folded card gone soft with handling. Mira opened the card and found it written in small square letters, like a note left on a fridge. "For when I forget, which I do," it said. "My way home is behind the lantern bracket at the tunnel mouth: push hard on the left, and mind your head." At the bottom was one more line, in pencil, which said only: "Gone, but not lost." Mira read it twice. Then she put the card back exactly as she had found it, because its owner had been standing here an hour ago, and went on down to the tunnel.

choices.label: Go down to the tunnel.

nodes.body: The service shaft dropped straight down through the tower. Iron staples had been driven into one wall to make a ladder, each one a cold hoop just wide enough for a boot. Beside them hung a knotted rope, running up over a pulley, the kind keepers use for hauling oil cans. Mira leaned out and tugged a staple, which did not move. She tugged the rope, and it held too, but it creaked, and a little puff of fibre drifted down past her into the dark. There was no seeing the bottom.

choices.label: Climb down the iron staples.
Try her weight on the knotted rope.

nodes.body: The iron staples were so cold they burned. Mira climbed down them one at a time, never letting go of one until she had tight hold of the next, and counted under her breath to keep her breathing slow. "Thirty, thirty-one, do not look, thirty-two," she told the wall. At fifty her boot met a floor that did not ring, and she found herself in a low undercroft with sweating walls, shaking arms and rust on both palms. Ahead of her a round brick tunnel mouth breathed cold air, in and out.

choices.label: Step into the tunnel mouth.

nodes.body: Mira wrapped both hands round the knotted rope and tried her weight on it, a little at a time. It held her. It also creaked, a small dry sound, and she felt one of the strands inside it part with a tick against her palm. The staples were an arm's length away to her right. "Do not even think about it," she told the rope, without much hope. It would be so much faster. It hung straight down the middle of the shaft like an invitation, turning slightly, and another puff of fibre came sifting down past her face.

choices.label: Let go of the rope and use the staples.
Swing out and slide down the rope.

nodes.body: Mira let go of the rope and reached across for the first of the staples. She was four rungs down when the rope gave up without any help from her. It parted somewhere above with a soft pop, and the whole length of it came whipping past her shoulder and went on falling for what seemed a long time. The thump, when it came, was a very long way down. "Okay, good," Mira said in a small voice, to the staple in front of her nose. She climbed the rest with great care, and stepped off at the bottom into a low undercroft where a brick tunnel mouth breathed cold air.

choices.label: Step into the tunnel mouth.

nodes.body: The outer ladder ran straight down the side of the tower, bolted to the stone. Mira swung onto it, and at once the fog took everything away. She could not see the ground, or the top, or her own boots, only her hands, white on a wet iron rung. The rungs were slick, and the wind pulled at her jacket in long steady tugs. It was a great deal further down than it had looked from the door, and her arms had already begun to notice.

choices.label: Go down slowly, one rung at a time.
Go down fast before her arms give out.

nodes.body: Mira went down slowly, like a very old person getting into a cold bath. One hand, one foot, the other hand, the other foot, and never two of them moving at once. "Three on, one off," she said to the rungs. "Three on, one off." It took a long time, and it was the right amount of time. When her boot finally found rock she stood holding the ladder until her knees stopped arguing. A low opening showed in the foot of the tower, out of the wind, and behind it a round brick tunnel mouth breathed cold air.

choices.label: Step into the tunnel mouth.

nodes.body: The tunnel was brick, low and round, and it ran out under the rock toward the sound of the sea. A storm lantern hung on an iron bracket just inside, with a box of matches on the ledge beside it. Its glass was still warm. Mira lit it, and the yellow light showed her three ways on. One branch ended at a heavy door bound in brass. One opened into a wide dark room that smelled of tar and new wood. The third ran downhill to an iron gate, with the tide sighing in and out behind its bars. On the floor, a line of wet bootprints came out of the dark and stopped dead at the bracket.

choices.label: Go to the brass-bound door.
Go into the room that smells of tar.
Go down to the iron sea gate.
Feel behind the bracket for the keeper's way.

nodes.body: The door at the end of the branch was oak, bound in brass, with a little tower burned into the wood. It had an iron lock the size of a loaf, far too big for any small key. Its own great key hung beside it on a hook, rusted the colour of a fox. To the left of the door a side passage ran off round the corner of the room, but a roof beam had come down across it, thick as Mira's waist. Only a low gap was left underneath. Dust lay on everything here, and nobody had touched that key in a long time.

choices.label: Try the rusted key in the lock.
Look at the beam across the side passage.

nodes.body: The rusted key went into the lock with a crunch and turned half a circle as sweetly as a tap. Then it stopped. Something inside had seized, and the key stood out of the lock at a slant, quivering slightly, with all of Mira's strength making no difference to it. "Half a turn more," Mira breathed at it, "is all I am asking." She let go and shook out her fingers. A few drops of oil from the lantern's filler cap would loosen it, given time to soak in. One hard shove was quicker, and the key was old iron, and old iron did not always bend before it broke.

choices.label: Oil the lock and give it time.
Shove the key round hard.

nodes.body: It took time, and more patience than she liked. Then something gave with a soft clunk, and a door that had been shut for a year swung inward under Mira's hand. Stale, cool air came out to meet her, smelling of old paper and candle wax. She stood on the threshold with the lantern held up, and for a moment she did not go in. It felt like opening somebody's diary. "I am only looking," Mira said to the dark room, and it did not say she could not.

choices.label: Step into the keeper's room.

nodes.body: Mira shoved the key round hard. It went another finger's width with a noise like a nail on a slate, and then it stuck fast, tighter than before. Now it would not go forward and it would not come back. She could feel something thin inside the lock bending against it, like a wishbone just before it snaps. Her hands were shaking with the effort of not shoving again. Slowly, like somebody putting down a thing that might go off, she took them away from the key.

choices.label: Ease the key back a hair at a time.
Put her whole weight on the key.

nodes.body: She eased the key back a hair, and rested, and eased it another hair, with her tongue between her teeth and the lantern hissing at her elbow. It was the slowest thing she had ever done. Somewhere in the third minute the bent thing inside the lock sprang straight again with a tiny ping, and the key, all of a sudden, was only a key. Mira turned it gently the rest of the way, and the lock went over with a clunk like a full stop. The door of the keeper's room moved under her hand. "Sorry," she told it, "and I will be nicer."

choices.label: Push the door open and go in.

nodes.body: The beam had come down out of the roof and jammed across the side passage, one end on the floor and the other wedged against the wall at the height of Mira's hip. Beyond it she could see the passage bend round the corner of the keeper's room toward a second, smaller door. The gap under the beam was just about the size of a girl lying flat. An iron bar leaned against the wall nearby, left over from some long-ago repair. The beam creaked when she put her hand on it, and a thread of grit ran down from the roof.

choices.label: Lever the beam aside with the iron bar.
Lie flat and wriggle under the beam.

nodes.body: Mira fitted the iron bar under the low end of the beam and leaned on it, a little at a time. The beam groaned, shifted, and rolled against the wall with a thud that she felt through her boots, and then it lay still and out of the way. Round the corner the side passage ended at a small door with a tower burned into it. Fresh bootprints passed that door in the dust, going on toward a stair, and Mira stared at those for a long moment. But the door had only a latch, stiff with salt, and no lock at all.

choices.label: Take her time with the stiff latch.

nodes.body: The room that smelled of tar was a store, stacked to the brick roof with crates and barrels, and not one of them had a mark on it to say where it had come from. On a shelf by the door a grey radio set glowed faintly, hissing to itself, with no microphone and nothing to talk into. As Mira lifted the lantern, the hiss cleared its throat. "Tower," said a man's voice, soft and patient, "I see you blinking, old man, a whole year of blinking, and I can wait longer than you can walk." Then there was only the hiss again. A small iron ledger box sat on the lid of the nearest crate.

choices.label: Prise the lid off a crate.
Open the iron ledger box.

nodes.body: The lid of the crate came up with a squeal of nails. Inside, packed in straw, were bolts of fine cloth and tins of tobacco and squat brown bottles with foreign labels, all of it a year old at least and furred with dust. Nobody had opened this crate since the night it was landed. Mira counted the stacks around her and stopped at sixty. "He has got a whole shop down here," she whispered, "and he cannot come and fetch it." The radio hissed on its shelf. At the back of the store a low doorway led on, deeper under the rock.

choices.label: Duck through the low doorway.

nodes.body: The iron box was not locked, and inside it lay a ledger, bound in oilcloth, whose pages Mira turned under the lantern. Six winters of fog nights ran down the left-hand side. Beside each was a count of crates landed and the letter V. The column for goods taken away was empty, every line of it, and for the last year there were no entries at all, only blank ruled paper. "It all came in," Mira said, "and none of it went out, and then a year of nothing." She looked at the radio. At the back of the store a low doorway led on, deeper under the rock.

choices.label: Leave the ledger in its box and duck through the low doorway.

nodes.body: Beyond the low doorway a narrow passage ran on between sweating bricks. Mira had gone ten steps along it when a cold draught came up from somewhere and laid the lantern flame flat. It shrank to a blue bead. The dark jumped in close, and with it came the feeling that the radio's patient voice had followed her down the passage. The wick wanted trimming, that was all. A paler patch showed ahead, not far off, in the shape of a door. The flame fluttered, and steadied, and fluttered again.

choices.label: Hurry on toward the paler patch.
Stop and trim the wick.

nodes.body: Mira set the lantern down, pinched the wick straight to trim it, and shielded it with both hands until the flame stood up tall and yellow. The passage came back. So did something she would have walked straight past: chalk on the bricks beside her, a long row of tally marks under the words "Landed, fog," each with a V beside it. A second row was headed "Taken away," and there was not one mark in it. "All in and none out," she said, "so he has never dared come back for it." Ahead, the paler patch was a door with a tower burned into the wood, its latch rusted through.

choices.label: Go through the door with the tower on it.

nodes.body: The branch ran downhill to an iron gate that closed the tunnel from wall to wall. Beyond its bars a slipway slid down into the sea, and the sea was coming up it, each swell a little higher than the last. To the right, just past the gate, a stone ledge ran above the water toward a flight of steps. Out in the fog, low on the water, a small yellow light hung perfectly still. It could not be a buoy, because buoys rock with the swell, and this one did not move at all. "And what are you waiting for?" Mira asked it under her breath. She put her face to the cold bars and stared at it, and the tide wet the toes of her boots.

choices.label: Work the gate open and take the ledge.
Wade down the slipway for a closer look.

nodes.body: The gate ground open a hand's width at a time, shrieking on its hinges, until there was room to slip through sideways onto the ledge. The stone was wet and green and sloped toward the water. A swell came up the slipway, slopped right over the ledge around her ankles and pulled at them, then hissed and fell back. Between swells the ledge drained and shone. The steps were ten paces away, and they were the worst ten paces Mira had ever looked at. A row of rusty iron rings ran along the wall at hand height. She gripped the first ring so hard that it hurt, and counted the swells in and out, and her knees would not keep still.

choices.label: Go now, between two swells.
Hold the ring until the big ones pass.

nodes.body: Mira let go of the ring and went. Three paces along, her boot shot sideways on the slime, and she grabbed the next ring with both hands just as a swell came over the ledge. It was up to her knees in a moment, cold enough to stop her breath, and it pulled at her legs as if it wanted them. She hung on with her eyes shut until it drained away. After that she went ring to ring, never letting go of one until she had hold of the next, and she was soaked and gasping by the time she crawled up the steps. "Never again," she told the sea, and meant it. At the top of the steps was a door.

choices.label: Push open the door at the top.

nodes.body: Mira held the ring and let three big swells come and go, each one slopping over the ledge and tugging at her boots. While she waited, the lantern showed her the wall beside it. The stone was covered in chalk, a long row of tallies under the words "Landed, fog," each with a V beside it. A second row was headed "Taken away," and it had no marks in it at all. "All in and none out," Mira said, mostly to stop her teeth chattering. Then the sea drew a long breath and the ledge drained, and she went ring to ring with her face to the stone, never letting go of one until she had hold of the next. A swell caught her on the last pace and soaked her to the knees. She scrambled up the steps on her hands, shaking, to a door.

choices.label: Go in through the door at the top.

nodes.body: Behind the bracket the bricks were only painted wood. Mira pushed, and a door no higher than her chin swung into a dry, narrow passage that was on nobody's plan but the keeper's own. The wet bootprints went along it in a line, every one pointing away from her. Twenty steps in, the passage forked. To the left was a small door with a tower burned into the wood, which could only be the back way into the keeper's own room. To the right a stair climbed toward cold air and the smell of heather, and the bootprints went up it, still wet. "That is his way out," Mira said, "and he has only just used it."

choices.label: Follow the bootprints up the stair.
Open the small door into the keeper's room.

nodes.body: The stair came up through a trapdoor in the heather, behind the headland, and the bootprints went on from it along a sheep track, dark in the dew. The fog was thin up here and turning grey with morning. Far ahead, a figure with a lantern was walking inland, slow and stiff. Only one person had any reason to use the keeper's own way, and Mira did not try to catch him up. She only meant to see where he went, so that she could tell the harbour office exactly where to look. So she kept well back on the open track, through one gate and then a second, past a bog that sucked at the edges of the path. The lantern went out as the sky grew light. At last the track came down into a fold of the hills, where a low stone cottage stood with smoke just beginning to rise from its chimney.

choices.label: Knock, then step back to the gate.

nodes.body: Beyond the door, the keeper's room was small and snug and perfectly dry, with the sea muttering somewhere beyond its walls. A bunk stood along one side, its blanket folded square. There was a stove, a shelf of books, a pipe rack with one pipe missing, and an empty brass hook with a label under it that said "Lamp key." A year of dust lay over all of it. On the desk, propped against a candlestick, stood an envelope sealed with red wax. "To whoever followed the light," Mira read aloud. Her legs ached. It was long past midnight. Somewhere back along the tunnel was a room that smelled of tar, and over her head were two lamps, one small and busy and one great and dark. Two miles off there was a bus shelter with a bench in it.

choices.label: Pick up the sealed letter.
Find the store that smells of tar.
Climb back up toward the lamps.
Leave it all and start for the bus shelter.

nodes.body: The sealed letter was heavier than it looked, and the wax of the seal had a little tower pressed into it. Mira turned it over. There was nothing on the back at all. She slid a thumbnail under the flap and stopped. It was addressed to her, in a way, since she was the one who had followed the light. But a letter from a missing man was also exactly the kind of thing a harbour master would want to open himself, with witnesses, and with the wax still whole. Her jacket had a deep inside pocket with a button. The wax was brittle and dark, like a boiled sweet, and it would only take a second to break.

choices.label: Break the seal and read it.
Button it into her jacket unopened.

nodes.body: The seal broke with a snap, and the letter began with the weather. "Fog," wrote Ferris, "and my last night as keeper. For six winters I took a man's money to look away while he landed cargo under my light. Now he wants the tower too, and I have run. But I will come back each fog night and set his own lamp blinking, which in his code means keep off, and he will not dare land while it blinks. If you are reading this, you saw it. You are the first." Three more things were pinned behind the page: a map of the moor with a cottage marked, a confession signed and dated, and a last sheet headed "What I ask of you."

choices.label: Unfold the map of the moor.
Read the signed confession.
Read the last sheet.

nodes.body: The map was drawn in pencil on the back of a tide table. A dotted line left the headland by a trapdoor in the heather and wandered inland across the moor, past a bog marked "mind this" and two gates, to a square labelled "shepherd's cottage, mine now." It was a walk of an hour, perhaps a little more, and the sky would be going grey by the time she climbed out. At the bottom Ferris had added something smaller. "If you would sooner send grown men with lanterns, I shall not blame you. The harbour office opens at six."

choices.label: Walk to the cottage on the moor.
Take the map to the harbour office.

nodes.body: The cottage door was painted blue, a long time ago. Mira knocked, and then stepped back down the path to the gate, with the whole open hillside behind her. Inside, a chair scraped, and then everything went very still. "If he sent you, the man with the grey boat," said a voice from behind the door, "you can tell him I have said nothing, not a word, to anyone, in a whole year." It was an old voice, and it was trying hard not to shake. "Nobody sent me," Mira said, and after that there was a long pause, in which a sheep coughed somewhere up the hill and a bolt rattled but did not slide. "Then how," said the voice, more quietly, "did you ever come to find my light?"

choices.label: Tell him about the bus.
Tell him the light says keep off.
Tell him to stay bolted in while she fetches help.

nodes.body: "I missed the last bus," Mira told him. "By four minutes. So I was on the headland in the fog, and I saw it blinking, and I went to look." Nothing happened for so long that she thought he had gone away. Then the voice said, "A bus," in a wondering sort of way, and after that it began to laugh, a rusty, creaking laugh that had not been used for a long time. "A year I have waited for a constable or a coastguard," it said, "and I get a girl who missed a bus." A bolt slid back, and then another.

choices.label: Wait for the door to open.

nodes.body: "Your light says keep off," Mira told him. "Steady, he lands, and blinking, he keeps off, and it was blinking, so I went to see who was telling him." Something bumped softly against the other side of the door, as if a forehead had been laid on it. "You read it," the voice said. "Forty-three nights I have hung that message in the fog, and the only soul who ever read it besides him is standing on my step, and she came toward it and not away." There was a long breath, in and out, and then a bolt slid back, and another.

choices.label: Wait for the door to open.

nodes.body: "Stay bolted in," Mira told him, "because you do not have to open it to me, and I am going to fetch the harbour master up here so that you can open it to them." The voice did not answer at once. "That is the most sensible thing anyone has said to me in a year," it said at last. "Ask for whoever is on the desk, and tell them Ferris, and tell them the light." Mira had already turned to go when it added, "And girl, mind the bog by the second gate, for it has had better folk than you." Mira minded the bog.

choices.label: Run for the harbour office.

nodes.body: The confession was one page, and it did not make excuses. "I, R. Ferris, keeper of this light, took money from a man named Varley for six winters, to see nothing and say nothing," it began. Each payment was listed with its date. "I never spent it. It is under the hollow step on the winding stair, every note. That does not make me honest. It makes me a coward who kept the receipts." At the bottom he had signed his name in full, and under the signature he had pressed his thumb in ink, so that nobody could say afterwards he had not meant it.

choices.label: Carry the confession to the town.

nodes.body: "What I ask of you," said the last sheet, "is three things, and you may refuse them all. Tell the town I am sorry, and tell them the light was never a ghost. And if a fog night ever comes when the pale light does not blink, know that I am too old or too ill to walk the moor, and wind the clockwork for me, which wants forty turns and is not hard." Mira read it standing up. Far above her, through all that stone, she imagined she could hear the shutter ticking, and for the first time all night the sound seemed friendly.

choices.label: Take up the keeper's task.

nodes.body: Mira took her thumbnail away from the wax and left the letter unopened. "Not mine," she said, though it nearly was. She found a clean page in the back of her homework diary and folded it round the envelope, so that the seal would not crack. Then she buttoned the whole thing into the inside pocket of her jacket, where she could feel its corner against her ribs. For a moment she stood in the keeper's room, looking at the bunk and the pipe rack and the empty hook. Whatever the letter said, it had been written by somebody who made his bed.

choices.label: Carry the sealed letter out.

nodes.body: The store that smelled of tar was forty steps back along the tunnel, and it was bigger than Mira's school hall. Crates stood stacked to the brick roof in rows, with alleys between them, and every one was furred with a year of dust. A grey radio set hissed on a shelf by the door. "Still blinking," said a man's soft voice out of the hiss, to nobody, and then, "I can wait." Mira stood very still until the hiss came back. Her phone had forty per cent left. At the far end of the store the alleys ran on into darkness, where something heavy had once been dragged, long enough ago that the marks were furred with dust.

choices.label: Photograph the crates.
Follow the drag marks deeper.

nodes.body: Mira photographed the crates and the dust on them, the radio on its shelf, and the inside of one crate with its bottles and tobacco, and then all of it again with the flash, in case. Forty-one pictures. Nobody could say she had dreamed it now. But pictures on a phone with no signal were only pictures, and the man on the radio was still out there in the fog, a mile off, waiting for a light to change. Above her head the clockwork ticked. The lamp that reached the whole coast went on saying the same thing, over and over.

choices.label: Flash three short, three long, three short.
Carry the phone to the harbour master.

nodes.body: The drag marks led deeper, round the last stack to a low arch, and through the arch into a second room that was on nobody's plan. This one was not for crates of cargo. It was for the best of it: small chests, rolled carpets, a row of clocks, a tray of rings. The man on the radio had been skimming his own shipments and squirrelling the cream away down here in a hoard. "Oh, you greedy man," said Mira. On top of the nearest chest, on a square of black velvet, sat a jewelled compass no bigger than a plum, set all round with green stones that drank the lantern light and gave it back.

choices.label: Photograph the whole hoard, touching nothing.
Reach for the jewelled compass.
Count the crates against the tallies.

nodes.body: Mira put her hands in her pockets, so as to be sure of touching nothing, and took them out only to work the phone. She photographed each chest of the hoard where it stood, and each lid as she found it, open or shut. She photographed the dust, because dust was a kind of calendar, and the single line of old drag marks lying under it. When a carpet had slumped across a clock, she left it slumped. It took most of an hour and nearly all her battery. At the end she had sixty-three pictures and had not moved so much as a ring.

choices.label: Take the pictures to the harbour master.

nodes.body: Up close the jewelled compass was the prettiest thing Mira had ever been within reach of. Its needle swung and settled, pointing straight through the wall at the sea. It would fit in her fist. It would fit in her pocket, and one small heavy thing with green stones on it would make a harbour master sit up faster than any number of photographs. The lantern hissed. The velvet was very black. Her hand was already above the compass, and nobody in the whole world knew where she was.

choices.label: Slip the compass into her pocket.
Leave it on its velvet and photograph it.

nodes.body: Mira climbed back up to the little chamber of mirrors. The shutter was still at it, tick, tick, clack, on and off. Now that she was not frightened of it she could see how the whole thing worked, the lantern and the jar of weed and the clockwork arm, and she could see that it was only borrowing the tower. A stair led on up from here to the lamp room, where the great lamp had stood dark for a year. The little lamp had a great deal to say. The big one had not said anything in a long time.

choices.label: Climb to the great lamp.
Study the little lamp's shutter.

nodes.body: The great lamp filled the top of the tower like a glass beehive, and Mira walked round it twice. The oil tank was a third full, and the wick, when she pinched it, was soft and good, so that everything it needed was here except the turning. Its clockwork sat in a brass case beside it, with a square socket the size of a coin where a winding key should go. Nothing was in it. "Square," Mira said to the lamp, and looked at the socket for a long moment. The gears behind the socket were stiff with a year of salt, but her fingers just went round the biggest one, and it gave a very little when she pushed.

choices.label: Wind the clockwork with the brass key.
Force the big gear round by hand.
Take her hand off the gear and go back down.

nodes.body: Mira took her hand off the gear. Scratched into the brass beside the empty socket, small and square, were four words she had missed: "Key hid. Be patient." She read them and laughed once, not very happily. Somewhere in the cottage or the boathouse, down in the caves or behind some mirror, there was a key that fitted this socket, and she had walked straight past it. She went back down the stair to the little lamp, which needed no key at all and was still, patiently, saying its piece.

choices.label: Look hard at the little lamp's shutter.

nodes.body: The brass key slid into the square socket as if it had been waiting there all year. Mira wound the clockwork slowly, the way a stiff old thing likes to be wound, until the key would turn no more. Inside the case, gears that had not moved in a year began to tick, heavy and even, like a big dog's heartbeat. She trimmed the wick with her fingernails, struck a match from the box on the sill, and held it to the lamp. The flame caught and climbed. Then the great lens took hold of it and threw it out of the tower in a single white bar, so bright that the fog seemed to step back. The little green light below went on blinking for a moment, like someone still talking after the door has opened.

choices.label: Watch the beam go out to sea.

nodes.body: The little lamp's shutter was a square of tin on a brass arm, and the clockwork lifted and dropped it once every four seconds. Mira watched the whole rig for a long time. Beside the motor was a lever with two positions, marked in scratched letters "clock" and "hand."
