Pushed to "hand," it would let the arm swing free, so that a person with a message to flash might work the shutter herself. The lantern behind it burned on, steady and bright. A light like this reached a long way in fog. It reached the harbour, and it reached anyone out on the water.

choices.label: Flash three short, three long, three short.
Draw the whole rig in her notebook.

nodes.body: Mira meant to leave it all, the letter and the lamps and the store, because she was tired in a way that had got into her bones. She had found a secret stair, a clockwork ghost and a room under the sea, and what she wanted now, more than answers, was a bench in a bus shelter and both her eyes shut. The way out was long, though, and it had more turnings than she had noticed coming in. There was a stub of chalk on the keeper's desk. The journal was under her arm, too, and she did not remember picking it up again.

choices.label: Start for the bus shelter at once.
Pick up the chalk and mark the way.

nodes.body: Mira started for the bus shelter with one last look round the keeper's room, at the square-folded blanket and the letter on the desk, and she left them as they were. "I will tell somebody," she promised the room, "in the morning, when I can talk in sentences." Then she went the long way, up through the tower and out into the fog, with her hands pushed deep in her pockets. Behind her the pale light went on blinking over the sea. It looked different now that she knew it was a lantern on a shelf. It looked like somebody waiting up.

choices.label: Walk to the bus shelter.

nodes.body: The chalk was soft and yellow and wrote well on brick. Mira drew her first arrow to mark the way on the wall outside the keeper's door, big enough for a tired grown-up with a torch to find. The journal was a different problem. On the desk beside the letter, open at the right page, it would explain everything to whoever came down here next. Under her arm, it would be in the harbour office by breakfast, and nobody would have to come down here at all to believe her. She turned it over in her hands. It was heavier than a book that size had any right to be.

choices.label: Leave the journal open on the desk.
Carry the journal out with her.

nodes.body: Mira took the drawer by its handle and wrenched. The front came away in her hand with a crack like a snapped ruler, and the rest of the drawer jammed crooked in the desk, tighter than any lock. Through the split she could see a bundle of oilcloth, and poking out of it the bow of a brass key with a tiny tower stamped on it. Her fingers went in as far as the second knuckle and no further. "Oh, come on," she said. She tried the letter-opener, then a ruler, then a hairgrip from her own pocket. She was still trying when the window turned grey and the pale light, along with the last of the fog, blinked itself out.

Mira yanked the jammed brick out of the way, and the chimney let go. A slide of soot and broken firebrick came down into the grate with a long soft roar, and when the cloud cleared the hollow had gone, bundle and all, under a heap as high as her knees. She looked like the ghost of a chimney sweep. "Brilliant," she said, and sneezed black. She dug with the coal shovel until her arms shook, and near dawn the shovel rang on a flat stone where somebody had chalked three words in small square letters: "Gently does it." Mira sat down in the soot and laughed until she coughed.

Mira leaned out on the rail for a better look, and the rail leaned with her. A whole length of it tore out of the stone with a shriek and dropped away into the fog, and she threw herself backward so hard that she landed inside the lamp room on her elbows. She counted two full seconds before she heard the splash. For a long time she sat with her back against the great lens and her knees drawn up, quite unable to stand. From there, through the gap where the rail had been, she watched a small yellow lamp far out at sea. Each time the tower blinked, the lamp dipped, as if it were nodding.

Mira waded straight down the middle of the passage, and for ten steps it was only cold. Then the floor dropped away under a swell, the sea came up to her ribs in one push, and it was all she could do to grab the ledge and haul herself onto it like a seal. "Stupid," she told her chattering teeth, "stupid, stupid." The tide filled the passage below her and stayed there for hours. But when the water was deepest the weed on the walls woke and lit the whole flooded cave green, and by that light she saw arrows scratched along the ledge, one after another, pointing inland. Somebody had marked the dry way for whoever came after.

Mira breathed out and forced her shoulders into the gap, and the gap kept them. She could not go forward. For one very long minute she could not go the other way either, and the only part of her that moved was her heart. Then she made herself breathe out again, all the way, and wriggled free a finger's width at a time, leaving some skin and one jacket button behind. She sat against the arch and shook. While she had been stuck, with her cheek pressed to the stone, she had heard something through it, slow and even: tick, tick, clack. There was clockwork inside this rock, and somebody had wound it since the sun went down.

Mira went up fast, and the cracked rung lasted exactly as long as it took her to trust it. Then it snapped. She came down past four rungs she did not touch and one she did, and landed flat on her back on a heap of old net with every bit of breath knocked out of her. Nothing was broken except the ladder, though one ankle had opinions about being stood on. So she lay there and looked straight up. Somebody had chalked the underside of the loft floor in big square letters, meant to be read from exactly here. "Steady, he lands," it said. "Blinking, he keeps off." Out in the fog, through the gaps in the planks, the light went on blinking.

Mira went back to wedge the banging door, and the wind got there first. It tore the door out of her hands and slammed it so hard that the whole boathouse jumped, and behind her the shelf of gear came down across the hatch in a roar of chain and rusty iron. It took her an hour to drag it clear. Halfway through, with her ear near the boards, she heard slow footsteps in the passage underneath, and an old man's voice. "Forty-three," it said, quite clearly, to nobody. "Forty-three nights, and not a soul." Mira shouted. The footsteps stopped, then hurried off, and when at last she got the hatch up there was only darkness under it, and the smell of a pipe.

Mira rattled the padlock, and a bell began to ring. It was somewhere above her, inside the tower, small and sharp and furious, jerking on a wire that ran from the low door up through the ceiling. She let go at once, but the bell went on. Overhead a chair fell over. Boots ran across a floor, a door slammed, and somebody went down a stair in a great hurry, away from her. Then, up the open panel stair, a faint green glow went out, and the whole tower was dark, and it stayed dark. Whoever had been keeping that light had taken her for someone else, someone worth running from, and Mira stood on the landing with nobody left to ask.

Mira stamped on the step, and the step gave way like a pie crust. Her leg went through to the knee. When she had finished saying "ow" she found her boot resting on something soft, and she reached down past it and brought up a bundle of envelopes tied with fishing line. There were dozens. Each was marked with a V and a date, each was fat with banknotes, and not one of them had ever been opened. "Somebody paid you," Mira said to the dark stair, "and you never even looked." Her ankle was swelling fast inside her boot. She sat there on the nineteenth step with a fortune in her lap that was not hers, listening to the light tick.

Mira swung out onto the rope, and it held her for exactly one heartbeat before it parted with a soft pop. She dropped the length of her own body, hit the staples with both arms and her chin, and clung there like a cat on a curtain while the rope went rattling away down the shaft. It was a long time before it landed. Her palms were skinned raw, and her arms would only take her up, not down. In the chamber of mirrors she wrapped her hands in her scarf and watched the little shutter work. Beside it stood an oil can with a column of dates chalked on it, one for each filling, and the newest of them was not yet a day old.

Mira went down fast, and the fourth rung was not where her foot expected it. Her boot skidded off wet iron into nothing. For a moment she hung by her hands alone, with the fog turning slowly under her, and then she found the rung again and climbed up the tower a great deal more carefully than she had come down. She lay on the floor of the chamber until her arms stopped trembling. Through the open door the fog tore, just once, and showed her the moor behind the headland. A small yellow lantern was crossing it, far off, going inland at a walk. Whoever lit the light was on their way to bed.

Mira put her whole weight on the key, and the key broke. The bow came off in her hand, and the rest stayed in the lock, snapped flush, where no fingers would ever get it out again. She said a word her mother did not know she knew. Then she knelt and put her eye to the gap by the hinge, with the lantern held high. She could see a bunk with its blanket folded square, and a desk, and on the desk an envelope propped against a candlestick. The writing on it was big enough to read from where she knelt. "To whoever followed the light," it said, and that was her, on the wrong side of two inches of oak.

Mira lay flat and wriggled, and she was halfway under the beam when it sighed and settled. It came down on the tail of her jacket and pinned it to the floor like a butterfly. She could not go on, and for a moment she could not get out either, until she slid her arms out of the sleeves and crawled clear without it. The beam sank the last hand's width onto her jacket and closed the gap. With her nose to the floor she had seen something, though. There were bootprints in the dust on the far side, large ones, and so fresh that their edges were still sharp. Somebody used that passage, and had used it within the hour.

Mira dragged the gate open a crack and waded down the slipway, and for nearly a minute the sea was politer than she deserved. Then a swell lifted her off her feet, turned her round, and put her against the bars with a mouthful of salt. She hauled herself through the gap and lay on the tunnel floor, coughing, soaked to the neck and shaking too hard to hold the lantern. But the swell had carried her high enough to see. A grey launch lay out there with one lamp showing, and a man stood in its bow with binoculars, looking not at her but at the tower. He was watching the light the way a driver watches a red one.

Mira slipped the compass into her pocket, and something under the velvet came with it. It was a wire as thin as a hair. Far off down the tunnel, toward the sea gate, a bell began to chime, bright and steady, the kind of sound that carries over water. Out in the fog an engine coughed and caught. Mira put the compass down so fast that she dropped it, and ran for the stair. By the time she had brought the harbour master, at first light, the little room was bare to the bricks. "A year he waited out there," the harbour master said, turning over the square of velvet, "and then somebody rang him in." Mira did not say who.

Mira forced the big gear, and it went round a quarter of a turn with a scream of dry brass. Then something inside the case let go. There was a bang and a rattle of loose teeth, and the cover plate jumped off its screws and rang on the floor, and after that the gear would not move at all. The great lamp would stay dark. With the cover off, though, she could see the square socket all the way in, and three words stamped in the brass around it: "Wind her slow." It had never wanted strength. It had wanted a key with a square end, and somewhere on this headland there was one.

The door opened on an old man in a keeper's jersey, thinner than he should have been, blinking at the morning. "Fog is lifting," he said, and then, "You will want to know why it was lit." He told her on the bench outside, with a mug of tea going cold in his hands. "A man paid me six winters to look away while he landed cargo under my tower. His lamp, his code: steady, he lands, and blinking, he keeps off. So every fog night for a year I have walked that moor and set his own lamp blinking, and he has not dared touch a crate. I hoped somebody would see it and come, but nobody is ever on that headland after the last bus." He looked at her. "Forty-three nights, and you are the first." Then he stood up stiffly and reached for his cap. "Come along. You and I are going to walk to the harbour office, and I am going to say all of that again to a man with a notebook."

The harbour office had only just unlocked its door when Mira came through it, out of breath and not very clean. The clerk on the desk was eating toast. "Old Ferris is dead, love, a year since," he said with his mouth full, when she had said the keeper's name. Mira shook her head. "He is on the moor," she said, "in the cottage past the second gate, and he has been lighting the lighthouse on every fog night." The toast went down on the blotter. Within the hour six men were climbing the sheep track with a stretcher they did not need, and by noon they came down again, walking slowly, with a thin old man in the middle of them. He stopped at the office door and looked at Mira for a long moment. "So you are the one who followed my light," he said, "and then had the sense to fetch help, which is more than most of us manage."

Mira carried the confession to the town in her inside pocket and put it on the harbour master's desk at six in the morning. He read it twice, and then he read it aloud to the constable. "Kept the receipts," the constable said, "every one, under a step, and that is not how a smuggler's man behaves but how a frightened one does." By evening the whole harbour knew two things. The first was that a man named Varley had some questions to answer. The second was that old Ferris had not run off with anything, and had spent a year walking the moor to keep a lamp blinking. By morning somebody had chalked three words on the sea wall: "The keeper kept."

Mira took up the keeper's task that same night, because there was nobody else to do it. She climbed to the chamber of mirrors and gave the clockwork forty turns, slowly, although it did not need them yet. Then, under the last line in the keeper's journal, she wrote one of her own: "Seen, and I will tell them you are sorry, and that it was never a ghost. Mira." In the morning she gave the harbour master the letter, map and all, and he fetched the old man down from the moor by noon. Three weeks later the fog came in again, and word came up from the harbour that the pale light had blinked all night over the sea, right on time. The old keeper was well, and the promise could wait.

Three short, three long, three short. Mira ran up to the chamber of mirrors, found a lever marked "hand" beside the clockwork, and flashed the call with the shutter until her arm ached. On the ninth time a white light answered from the harbour mouth, long and slow. On the twelfth an engine was coming, a big one. Out on the water a small yellow lamp tried to slip away north, and found a coastguard cutter lying across its bows with every lamp lit. "Lighthouse, lighthouse," a voice boomed over the water through a loudhailer, "we have your signal, so stay where you are, keeper, and stay warm." Mira looked round the little chamber for a keeper. Then she understood, and sat down, and laughed.

Mira carried the phone to the harbour master the moment his office opened, and he looked through forty-one photographs without saying a word. At the thirty-ninth he put on his glasses. "That is four hundred crates of somebody's bad conscience," he said, "so whose is it?" Mira told him about the soft voice on the radio that said it could wait. "He is out there now," she said, "in the fog, waiting for the light to change." The harbour master was already reaching for his coat. By nine the revenue men were at the tower, and by ten a grey launch was being towed in past the sea wall. "And what," he asked her, over the bacon sandwich he had bought her, "were you doing out there at midnight?" Mira swallowed. "I missed my bus," she said.

Mira took the pictures to the harbour master, all sixty-three, and he went through them with a magnifying glass. "You did not touch any of it?" he said. Mira shook her head. "Not a ring," she said, "because I kept my hands in my pockets." When the revenue men opened the little room that afternoon, it matched her photographs down to the slumped carpet and the old drag marks under the dust, and there was nothing a clever lawyer could say had been moved, or added, or dreamed. The jewelled compass was still on its velvet. Under it they found a wire as thin as a hair, running to a bell at the sea gate. "Somebody," said the harbour master, "was hoping you had sticky fingers."

Mira counted the crates against the tallies, row by row, with the lantern held high, and looked for a gap. There was none. The tallies had said crates in and none out, and here they all were, the big store and the little room together, with a year of dust lying on them as smooth as snow. She photographed the dust. At six she put the phone on the harbour master's desk and told him, "He has not touched any of it in a year, so something must be keeping him off." The harbour master looked out of his window at the headland for a long time. "Not something," he said, "but someone, because smugglers do not leave four hundred crates alone out of good manners." By dusk the revenue men were at the tower, asking very politely who had been lighting the lamp.

The beam went out to sea like a slow white arm, round and round, and Mira watched it from the lamp room window with the key still warm in her hand. Far off, a fishing boat answered with one long grateful blast of its horn. Nearer in, the beam swept over a grey launch with a single lamp, and the launch turned tail and ran for open water, because a lighthouse with a keeper in it is no place to land anything. Three miles inland an old man came to his cottage door and saw the sky over the sea turn white and dark and white again. He stood there a long while. Then he took his cap down from its nail, and for the first time in a year he set out for the tower without waiting for the fog. The hollow tower was hollow no more.

Three short, three long, three short. Mira pushed the lever to "hand" and worked the shutter herself, and the green light stopped saying keep off and began, for the first time, to say come. She flashed it until her wrist ached. Then a light answered from the harbour, and another beside it, and soon there was a whole string of them coming along the coast road, torches and headlamps and one blue flasher. They had been out since ten o'clock, as it happened, looking for a girl who had missed the last bus. "Mira?" somebody shouted up from the rocks, through cupped hands, "Mira, is that you up there?" She leaned out of the door. "It is me," she shouted, "and I have got a lot to show you."

Mira drew the whole rig in her notebook, every mirror and every angle, with arrows to show which way the light went. She drew the jar of weed and the lantern, and the clockwork with its brass arm, and she timed the shutter against her phone: four seconds on, four seconds off. It took two hours and eleven pages. By the end there was nothing left of the ghost of the Hollow Lighthouse but a neat diagram that any teacher would have given full marks. Then she put her hand on the clockwork to feel it run, and found the spring wound tight. That was the one thing she could not draw. Somebody had stood exactly here, a few hours ago, and wound it.

Mira carried the sealed letter out of the tower with one hand flat over her pocket, the whole way, as if it might jump. The fog was thinning by the time she reached the road, and the first bus of the morning came out of it with its lights on. She gave the letter to the harbour master at five past six, across his desk, with the seal unbroken. He turned it over twice. "To whoever followed the light," he read. "That would be you, I think, and not me." He pushed it back across the blotter with one finger, and beside it he laid a paper knife. "Go on," he said, "and I shall be your witness."

Mira left the compass on its velvet and took her hand away, and she photographed it from four sides without touching so much as the cloth. The flash showed her what the lantern had not. A wire as thin as a hair ran from under the compass, down the side of the chest, and away along the wall toward the sea gate, and at the far end of it, she had no doubt at all, there was a bell. "Oh, you sneak," she said to the man on the radio, wherever he was. It had been bait, the prettiest thing in the room, left on top for exactly her kind of fingers. She photographed the wire too. Then she walked out past all of it with her hands in her pockets, whistling, not very well.

Mira walked to the bus shelter and sat on its bench with her hood up, and she must have slept, because the next thing she knew a bus was standing there with its engine running. It was the same driver as last night. "You are out early," he said, as she counted coins into the tray. "I am out late," said Mira, "because I missed you last night by four minutes." He laughed, and then he looked past her, through the windscreen, at the headland. "Funny," he said, "for a second I thought there was a light in the old tower." Mira turned to look. The fog was lifting, and in the grey of the morning the pale light blinked once more, and went out.

Mira left the journal open on the desk, beside the letter, at the page with the sketch of the tunnel. Then she chalked her way out. She drew an arrow at every turning, big and yellow, up the tunnel and the stair and through the panel to the landing, so that nobody who came after her could possibly go wrong. At the foot of the tower she raised the chalk for the last one and stopped. There was an arrow there already. It was old and faint, drawn in the same yellow chalk by a taller hand, and it pointed straight at the panel. Somebody else had once stood here hoping to be followed. Mira drew hers beside it.

Mira carried the journal out with her, under her arm and then, when the wind got up, inside her jacket. It rode there all the way along the coast road like a hot-water bottle that had gone cold. At the first street lamp she stopped to look at it once more, to be sure it was real. It fell open at a column of dates. They were fog nights, every one, with the word "Blinking" beside each in small square letters, and they ran on for a whole year past the day the keeper vanished. The last of them was today's, and its ink came off on her thumb. Mira looked over her shoulder at the headland, and then she began to run toward the harbour office.
